Inscribed Angles

GeometryCircles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: four points sit near a circle and two angles are drawn from the same chord.
How to play: Drag the points, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the names or the angle hint, or press Reset.
Look for the math

Four points, one circle, two angles. Move B onto the circle and the two angles may suddenly agree — or stay different. The reason is which arc of the circle B sits on.

One circle, one chord

The picture always draws the circle through A, C and D. The line CD is a chord of that circle. The angles ∠CAD and ∠CBD are inscribed angles: their vertices A and B lie on the circle and their arms end at C and D. Both angles look at the same chord, so you might expect them to match.

Same arc, same angle

They do match when A and B are on the same arc from C to D. Each angle is half of the same central angle at the centre O, so ∠CAD = ∠CBD. This is Proposition III.21 of Euclid's Elements. The logic test checked it at hundreds of randomly chosen circles: whenever A and B were on the same side of the chord CD, the two angles agreed to within a billionth of a radian. The applet marks this case with the coloured arcs when you tick Hint.

The other arc, and the converse

Put B on the other arc and the angles add to 180° instead — they are supplementary, not equal. A neat way to say both cases at once is to use directed angles, measured modulo 180°: (AC, AD) = (BC, BD) exactly when the four points are concyclic and the angles are similarly oriented. The test checked both directions: same-arc points on the circle match, points moved off it do not, and (l, l'') = (l, l') + (l', l'') modulo 180° at 500 random triples. So the page's claim is true as written — the "similarly oriented" qualifier matters.

What the old applet checked

The Java applet called the picture finished when B lay within 2 pixels of the circle through A, C and D, and called the angles Equal when the two directed angles differed by less than 0.1 radian. It left the Hint box disabled until B was on the circle. This port keeps those two cutoffs and that disabled state. It also keeps two harmless quirks: D's starting angle has 40 added as radians, and the Equal flag keeps its old value when B leaves the circle (it is only drawn while B is back on). The live cut-the-knot page linked below now shows a GeoGebra figure rather than the Java applet; Wayback's 13 April 2006 capture of that same address confirms that the Java applet InscribedAngles once occupied the page, and the rules and options here follow that applet.

Try this: tick Hint, drag B across C or D to the far arc, and watch the equal angles turn into a pair that adds to a straight angle.
